topics.topic: Exact module-loading recipe, source path, observable import metadata, and cross-execution stability
questions: What exact importlib loading recipe, source path, and metadata must every execution expose, and must those observable values be identical across fresh executions?
What exact, stable values must path-bearing import metadata have in every fresh execution?
What exact import mechanism and observable metadata values must every execution use, and must paths be stable across fresh execution environments so equal inputs retain equal output digests?

quotes: It is loaded from its file in the exchange directory as `importlib` loads a source file, with the metadata `importlib` gives it, under the one fixed name `cabinet_sandbox_code`, which no module of the standard library has; the module is entered in `sys.modules` under that name before its body runs and stays there until the execution ends, so code that looks its own module up by name (`dataclasses` under postponed annotations, `typing.get_type_hints`) behaves as it does under an import.

Every function execution, in trial and in a run alike, runs in a fresh isolated environment created by the sandbox: Linux `bubblewrap` with new user, PID, IPC, UTS and network namespaces, no network interface but the namespace's own loopback — up, as bubblewrap leaves it in a new network namespace, and reaching nothing outside the execution, so K-02's "no network" holds; this is a property of how the kernel starts bubblewrap, which the kernel does not inspect or verify at run time — the start check (rule 8) asks only that a probe execution succeeds — an environment holding only `PYTHONHASHSEED=0` (rule 2), a read-only runtime, and one private exchange directory in which every file the code writes is bounded by `sandbox_scratch_bytes_max` (rule 5).
The same implementation on the same input yields the same output digest twice.
judgement.divergence: One implementer uses a stable source such as `/exchange/cabinet_sandbox_code.py` and SourceFileLoader-derived metadata; another uses a different stable source path or importlib construction with different `__file__`, `__cached__`, `__loader__` or `__spec__.origin`; an author whose trial expects one metadata value sees admission and activation versus `output_mismatch` and refusal.
judgement.why: The repeatability test requires stable observable results but neither State 2 nor the later texts fixes the source filename, complete importlib recipe, cache policy or exact metadata values.

witness.initial: A contract has no inputs, one string output, and a trial case whose expected output is `/exchange/cabinet_sandbox_code.py`; its implementation returns `__spec__.origin`.
events: An authoring agent submits the implementation, causing admission to execute it in a fresh sandbox.
outcomes: The loader uses `/exchange/cabinet_sandbox_code.py` as the stable origin, so the trial passes and the implementation is admitted and activated.
The loader uses another stable source path permitted by the text, so the returned origin differs and admission is refused with `output_mismatch`.
witness.observer: The submitting agent sees admitted and activated versus refused.
basis: An implementation is a Python module that defines a top-level function `run` taking one argument, a dict with one entry per input port, and returning a dict with exactly one entry per output port.

Submitting an implementation — new, or equal to an existing one — runs admission unless an AdmissionVerdict M08 for that implementation and the current corpus digest already exists, in which case that verdict is used.

A case passes when the execution succeeded and, if the case states expected outputs, every output's digest equals the expected one — a file output is recorded in the TrialExecution by digest, size and media type, keeps no bytes, and is compared with the expected file fixture by digest; a `many` file output equals its expected list when both have the same length and the digests are equal position by position, so order and repetitions count; outputs that validate but differ are `output_mismatch`.

After size, token and depth checks, are discovery requests validated against their own MCP method schemas and capable of `invalid_request`, or must every known-token discovery request be answered regardless of its fields?

After size, configuration/token and depth checks, must discovery requests also pass method-specific schema and unknown-field validation, or must every authenticated discovery request receive an answer regardless of its remaining shape?

topics.topic: Required handling of implementation mutation of the fixed sys.modules entry
questions: Is “stays there” guaranteed against mutation by implementation code, merely a promise that the runner itself will not remove it, or is deletion/replacement a sandbox violation or crash?

Must the sandbox prevent, reverse or otherwise classify an implementation's deletion or replacement of `sys.modules['cabinet_sandbox_code']`, or does "stays there" describe only what the runner does when code does not mutate it?
Must the entry remain present and point to the original module despite mutations by implementation code, or does “stays there” mean only that the runner itself does not remove it?

quotes: It is loaded from its file in the exchange directory as `importlib` loads a source file, with the metadata `importlib` gives it, under the one fixed name `cabinet_sandbox_code`, which no module of the standard library has; the module is entered in `sys.modules` under that name before its body runs and stays there until the execution ends, so code that looks its own module up by name (`dataclasses` under postponed annotations, `typing.get_type_hints`) behaves as it does under an import.
A module using `dataclasses` under `from __future__ import annotations`, and one reading its own entry in `sys.modules`, load and conclude `passed`.
judgement.divergence: One runner prevents deletion or replacement of `sys.modules['cabinet_sandbox_code']`, so code observing the entry sees the original module or the mutation raises; another exposes ordinary mutable `sys.modules`, so deletion or replacement succeeds and changes the returned value or causes later annotation processing to crash; the submitting agent sees different trial output or outcome.
judgement.why: The text requires the entry to stay but specifies neither enforcement nor the execution outcome when untrusted code attempts to delete or replace it.

witness.initial: A contract has no inputs and one boolean output; its implementation deletes `sys.modules[__name__]` in the module body and `run` reports whether the fixed name remains present.
events: An authoring agent submits the implementation and admission loads its module in the sandbox.
The module body attempts to delete its fixed `sys.modules` entry before `run` is called.
outcomes: The runner protects the entry or rejects the mutation, producing true or a classified failure.
The runner exposes the ordinary mutable mapping, the deletion succeeds, and `run` returns false.
witness.observer: The submitting agent sees a different TrialExecution output or outcome and potentially a different admission verdict.
basis: An implementation is a Python module that defines a top-level function `run` taking one argument, a dict with one entry per input port, and returning a dict with exactly one entry per output port.

The runtime is one Python interpreter with its standard library and nothing else, fixed by the kernel release (State 0 questions 4 and 17: photo processing is the agent's own work outside the kernel), started with a fixed hash seed (`PYTHONHASHSEED=0`) so that set and dict ordering repeats.

Submitting an implementation — new, or equal to an existing one — runs admission unless an AdmissionVerdict M08 for that implementation and the current corpus digest already exists, in which case that verdict is used.

topics.topic: Initialize protocol-version negotiation, capabilities, and session-state requirements
questions: Which `initialize` requests are compatible, what version and capabilities are returned, and what happens when the requested protocol version is unsupported?
What protocol-version negotiation and session-state rules apply to `initialize`, and may `ping`, `tools/list` or catalogue operations be called before a successful initialization?

quotes: answer_request: [BEHAVIOR] The body is one JSON-RPC 2.0 message, parsed only after the depth check, which follows the size and token checks. A JSON object whose jsonrpc is "2.0" with a string method and an id is a request; one with a method and no id is a notification and one with no method a response: both are answered with empty bytes and change nothing. A request's method decides: initialize answers the result {protocolVersion: the imported MCP_PROTOCOL_VERSION constant, capabilities: {tools: {listChanged: false}}, serverInfo: {name: the imported MCP_SERVER_NAME constant, version: the imported MCP_SERVER_VERSION constant}} whatever version its params ask, and keeps no state; ping answers an empty result object; tools/list answers {tools: [...]} as below, ignoring any cursor; tools/call names the catalogue operation in params.name and carries its request in params.arguments, which then pass the remaining checks of the first note.

      streams: a POST to the path `MCP_ENDPOINT_PATH` carries one JSON-RPC
